#1670. Scotland's World Cup prize must not become a missed opportunity

Published: 15:23 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 15:36 EST, 23 November 2026

Confirmation that Scotland will co-host the 2035 FIFA Women’s World Cup is an undoubted boost for the game in this country.

Staging a global showpiece with England, Wales and Northern Ireland is indeed a potential game-changer.

The joint bid projected that the competition would attract 3.5billion viewers worldwide. And that 4.5m tickets would be sold across the host nations.

But the key for Scotland will be the impact it has on girls taking up the sport, supporters watching it and professionals playing it north of the Border.

Scotland captain Caroline Weir has already described it as a ‘pivotal’ moment, a ‘real opportunity’ to drive momentum and reach another level, domestically and internationally.

She’s right. It is an opportunity, of the once-in-a-lifetime variety, but a word of caution is in order. Opportunities are not enough in themselves to be transformative.

They have to be embraced, exploited and squeezed for all they are worth so that every last drop of their potential is properly fulfilled.

Star player Caroline Weir believes co-hosting the World Cup could be pivotal for women's football in Scotland

It would be criminal if the powers-that-be got complacent about this priceless gift and made assumptions about its long-term legacy.

More players, more fans and more media coverage would be hugely exciting, but it will all be wasted if not supported by facilities, coaches and the safeguarding that goes with it.

It has happened before. Interest in athletics rocketed after Glasgow 2014, but a poor infrastructure, which continued to rely on volunteers, prevented a grassroots boom.

And how many times have we heard Judy Murray complain that Scottish tennis squandered the opportunity presented to it by her son, Andy?

Scotland’s women played at the World Cup in 2019. Their game has grown since then, but the national side have not been to another major tournament and the domestic product is still a shadow of its English counterpart.

Only a handful of Scottish teams have full-time players. The wages are way behind those on offer down south. And professional men’s clubs could do much, much more to develop the sport. It’s no wonder the Scottish league can’t keep its better players.

The opposite is true in England, where the success of the national team is often attributed to the level of investment by the FA and the backing of sponsors across the country.

The good news is that Scotland have made a start on that front with something called Project 2035, which aims to transform girls' and women’s football over the next decade.

The Scottish government has stumped up an initial £250,000 to help with the 10-year plan, which outlined a number of key objectives earlier this month.

They want to grow participation at grassroots level, increase the number of women working in football - as coaches, leaders and decision-makers - and quadruple the number of fans. The hope also is that Scotland will progress beyond the group stage of at least one World Cup by 2035.

Having those ambitions is one thing; making good on them is quite another. The government, the league, clubs and the ruling body: all should be thrilled by this opportunity but they should also feel the pressure that it brings. For it is their responsibility, their duty, to make the most of it.

#1669. Aston Villa transfer news: How may Chelsea consider ending Alejandro Garnacho's deflating loan spell?

By Darren Plant | 27 Nov 2026 11:08

Chelsea are allegedly yet to determine whether they will consider ending Alejandro Garnacho's loan stint at Aston Villa.

On Tuesday evening, the Argentine was left out of the squad for the Champions League fixture at Galatasaray, despite Unai Emery naming two goalkeepers and having one spare spot on the substitutes' bench.

Emery suggested after the game that he only selected players who he felt were capable of making an impact in that particular match, essentially delivering a clear message to Garnacho.

Garnacho has been restricted to just seven substitute appearances totalling fewer than 100 minutes since making the loan switch to Villa, who can activate a permanent £43m transfer if the winger plays a set number of matches.

However, like in the case of Liverpool's Harvey Elliott in 2025-26, it has become apparent that Emery has given up on a loan player who Villa could sign for big money if they make in the region of eight to 10 appearances.

As per several reports, Villa do not have the option of ending Garnacho's loan during the winter transfer window, nor do Chelsea have a recall clause.

These were the same terms that Villa and Liverpool agreed for Elliott, and subsequently failed to agree over a compromise for the second half of the last campaign.

According to The Athletic, Villa will need to hope that a foreign club expresses an interest in signing Garnacho at the turn of the year.

Garnacho is said to have wanted to leave the Premier League for a European club prior to Emery expressing an interest in his services.

At this point in time, though, it is unclear whether Chelsea would give the green light to a change of clubs for Garnacho.

If it is not beneficial from a financial perspective, they may choose to take no action.

The exact reason why Emery wanted to sign Garnacho is unclear. The fact that the former Manchester United attacker has not made a single start is either reflective of his efforts in training or Emery not having any serious interest in a permanent deal.

Either way, it is clear that Garnacho needs to rebuild his career in Europe, most likely La Liga where he has previously spent time at Atletico Madrid as a youngster.

How that may come about remains to be seen. Any club would likely have to take the bulk of Garnacho's wages and pay a substantial loan fee for it to be worthwhile to Chelsea.

#1668. Newcastle 2-2 Arsenal: Two points dropped in a game of two halves

In the cold light of day, it’s hard not to look at what happened in the 45th minute of this game as a key moment. Arsenal were 1-0 up, well on top and absolutely deserving of the lead. Newcastle had struggled to exert any kind of control, and we’d already had 9 attempts on goal.

A good move down the left hand side saw Martin Odegaard square perfectly for Noni Madueke who arrived with pace, ready to finish first time. Unfortunately for him and for us, Lewis Hall produced a quite outstanding piece of defending to slide in and block the shot over the bar. That was the difference between Arsenal going in 2-0 up at the break rather than with just the single goal margin.

The lead had come via Eberechi Eze, finishing emphatically after superb work from Kai Havertz to rob the ball and play a deft pass behind the right back. Newcastle’s only chance had come early, a shot from Jacob Murphy that deflected off his own player and drifted wide with David Raya wrong-footed. After that, we bossed the half, with 11 shots in total, 65% possession, but still only that one goal.

It feels redundant to say this is a very, very good Arsenal team, but if we have a weakness, it’s that we don’t turn this kind of domination into more goals. Very often we don’t need to as our defensive solidity and consistency keeps the opposition at bay, but last night we let our standards slip in that regard, and the lack of firepower or being clinical in the final third came home to roost.

It was, very literally, a game of two halves. Newcastle made a triple sub at the break and it would be churlish not to give them credit for the fact it made a positive impact. However, the Arsenal performance was night and day. The opposition upped the energy and intensity, and we made mistakes. Odegaard miskicking a Riccardo Calafiori throw-in provided them the opportunity to equalise, and I do wonder why Harvey Barnes was so free at the back post to slide home for 1-1.

That goal gave them momentum, they caused us problems again and again, some of them of our own making with carelessness and misfortune. Eze got back well to defend in our box but unfortunately slipped, Raya’s clearance was unconvincing and then Gabriel had to boot the ball behind for a corner – from which they made it 2-1. Dan Burn drifted off Jurrien Timber to get a free header, the ball scrambled around a bit before Malick Thiaw poked it over the line to give them the lead. Messy, shambolic defending – not very Arsenal at all.

If we’re being fair, we have to say they could have scored again. David Raya went off with a shoulder injury, Kepa had to make a smart save at the feet of Lewis Miley but why was he one on one with the keeper in the first place? A Joe Willock shot deflected wide in similar fashion to the Murphy one in the first half, and eventually Arteta changed things with Christos Tzolis and Myles Lewis-Skelly coming on for Eze and Bruno Guimaraes who had a quiet return to his former club – bar that first half moment when he almost got enough contact on a fantastic Declan Rice cross but could only put the ball wide from close range.

We did get an equaliser, and very well worked it was too. We played the ball across the back line from right to left, into midfield where Havertz’s smart dummy allowed Odegaard room to drive on and find Madueke. He was Arsenal’s best attacking player last night, he kept trying to make things happen, and while I think the Newcastle keeper will probably have nightmares about letting that shot in, Madueke deserved the goal, and it earned us a point.

It was after the 90th minute when the manager brought on Viktor Gyokeres and Mikel Merino to try and find a winner, the Swede had one shot over the bar from the edge of the box, but had we found another, it would have been a real smash and grab. In the end, the draw was probably a fair result based on how the game played out, and afterwards the manager was unhappy at leaving two points behind:

My feeling is that we have lost two points today. And I say we because we were exceptional in the first half, from the beginning to the end. It should have been two, three or four-nil up, clear. But it wasn’t.

We started to lose duels, we started to lose second balls. We gave the ball away and have really poor circulation balls against their press and their waves. And when that happens, you give them belief.

It’s a pity because the margin should have been, again, much bigger for the level that we’ve shown.

And this is the key for me. It should have been, but it wasn’t, and it too often isn’t. As I said above, our defensive brilliance is fundamental to us winning so many games, but football is a game of variance. You can’t always control everything. On another night Odegaard just puts his foot through that throw in and that first Newcastle goal doesn’t happen. Eze and Raya deal better with that situation and we don’t concede a corner. We can focus on those individual things and say we could and should do better for sure, but you have to allow for some of that over the course of a season. You cannot be perfect for 90+ minutes 38 games in every league campaign.

The ongoing issue for me is our firepower though. I thought generally the front three played pretty well last night, and it’s not as if we missed a glut of chances, but it’s about turning the level of dominance we had in that first half into more goals. This isn’t a one-time issue either. We scored two lovely goals last night but we should have had that game firmly in our grasp at half-time, but in this league a single goal margin is never a sure thing.

The summer was a let-down in an attacking sense, there’s no getting away from that. If we had a forward line that was even close to our midfield and defence in terms of quality and depth, the Premier League would be a cakewalk. I know that’s a bit simplistic, but it’s also a fact. Regardless of what you think of the business, we let goals go to Turkey and Saudi Arabia, and replaced them with a player who has yet to score. Which isn’t to lay the blame at the feet of Tzolis, far from it, but with the squad planning/building that was undertaken.

For me, January becomes increasingly important because the improvement required is obvious, and for a sporting director whose track record looks quite hit and miss as it is, he needs a convincing window or the questions around the job he’s doing will become louder and louder, and for good reason.

The other big issue from yesterday was the injury to David Raya. It didn’t look good at all, and any absence for him would be a huge blow to the team. He’s been the best in the Premier League, and perhaps the best in Europe, for the last 18 months, and inevitably there’s a drop-off when any club is without their first choice keeper for any period of time. That’s another adjustment we’re probably going to have to make, and if it means we’re likely to be less secure and clean sheets are harder to come by, then that issue of scoring goals and being more potent comes into even sharper focus. Let’s keep fingers crossed it’s not as bad as it appears to be.

Right, I’ll leave it there for now. There’s plenty to unpick from this one, so I’ll leave you to it in the Arses. More here tomorrow, including an Arsecast Extra. Until then, have a great Sunday.

#1666. Mind the gap

Over the last few weeks, I’ve grown accustomed to waking up and experiencing low-level fear first thing in the morning. Today, it was a nice change not to be focused on my own health, and instead for my anxiety to centre around someone else – David Raya.

With any team or any squad there are players whose absence will be more keenly felt than others, but one of the things Arsenal have generally done really well in the last few years is close the gaps between ‘first choice’ and those behind them. It doesn’t mean there isn’t still a kind of hierarchy, just that you’re better able to cope if injury or suspension hits. Mikel Arteta referencing ‘finishers’ rather than substitutes might be a psychological ploy to keep his squad happy, but it’s more easy to apply when you have the group of players he has at his disposal.

If Jurrien Timber is out, we have Ben White. If Riccardo Calafiori can’t play, Piero Hincapie can. We all worried about William Saliba needing a long lay-off after the World Cup, but the arrival of Ezri Konsa offset that in exemplary fashion. If we miss Declan Rice, we have two World Cup winners, a Brazilian international, and one of the most highly regarded young English midfielders around to fill that gap. Further forward, Noni Madueke is performing at a level that makes Bukayo Saka’s absence feel less impactful than it would have previously, and while I think forward line quality remains an issue we need to solve as urgently as January, you can flip a coin between most of our options there without feeling you’ve weakened yourself considerably.

Unfortunately, I don’t think the same applies between the sticks. Raya has been the stand-out goalkeeper of the last few years, establishing himself as Arsenal’s number 1 after an initial settling in period. One, by the way, which I don’t think the manager handled particularly well. Typically he’s been near flawless in terms of his man-management, and while he was fundamentally right about wanting the Spaniard to come in and take the position to a new level, the way he fudged things around Aaron Ramsdale, talking about how he’d sub a goalkeeper in a game and all that nonsense really wasn’t his best moment. It left both of his keepers in a weird place for too long, until Raya’s confidence grew and his quality came to the fore.

Since then he’s won multiple golden glove awards, his shot-stopping has been incredible at times, and although every player and every keeper will make mistakes, his have been few and far between. For me though, despite the eye-catching acrobatics – which are more easily clipped up for the social media generation – his key asset is the assurance he brings to the team. Not just when he has the ball at his feet (even if there are times I would like him to move it more quickly), but how good he is from opposition set-pieces and crosses. He comes and claims and eases pressure time and time again, and I think that’s the thing we’re going to miss most if he’s out for any significant period of time.

Kepa is obviously a very experienced second choice, but is second choice for a reason. Realistically though, I don’t think there’s much any club can do to have a back-up option that’s nearly as good as their number 1. If you’re being brutally honest, many clubs in the Premier League don’t have a first choice that comes anywhere close to be as good as Raya, despite their best efforts and spending millions to try and find that player. So, as anxious as I am about him being out, it is one of those things we can’t really complain about. We just have to get on with it.

As I said in yesterday’s blog, we are probably going to be less secure at the back, that feels kind of inevitable, so the onus on the players further forward increases. Score more goals, turn that domination of possession and territory into more chances. If we have the ball in their half, our goalkeeper becomes something of a non-issue for as long as that’s the case. There are ways to cope, but we might need to gird our loins for some iffy moments at the back that we haven’t had to experience too often of late.

As Arsenal fans though, we’ve come through worse than this with goalkeepers in the past. I don’t want to give anyone PTSD first thing on a Monday morning, but when you’ve lived what we’ve lived in seasons gone by, hopefully a little Kepa period won’t be too traumatic. And maybe, after the scan, there’ll be better news about Raya than we expect. Fingers crossed.

Right, I have to leave it there for this morning. We will have an Arsecast Extra for you a bit later on though. We’ve already put out the call for questions on BlueSky @gunnerblog.bsky.social and @arseblog.com, so fire away using the hashtag #arsecastextra – or if you’re an Arseblog Member on Patreon, leave your question in the #arsecast-extra-questions channel on our Discord server.

Pod should be out around noon. Until then!

#1664. Arsenal vs Manchester City - prediction, team news, lineups

By Ben Knapton | 27 Nov 2026 11:24, Last updated: 27 Nov 2026 11:44

The stuttering champions and the challengers-in-crisis face off in Sunday's Premier League main event, which sees Arsenal and Manchester City draw swords at the Emirates Stadium.

The Gunners hold a six-point advantage over Enzo Maresca's men at the summit of the Premier League table, leading some to deduce that another success for the holders could already expel the Sky Blues from the title race.

Out of sight in first place, boasting the best defence in the top flight and taking 16 points from the last 18 on offer in the Premier League, Arsenal have lived up to their early-season expectations as the overwhelming favourites to retain their crown.

Yet, the Emirates faithful cannot shake the feeling that there is still something missing in Mikel Arteta's ranks, after Arsenal's second-half shortcomings were exposed in back-to-back draws with Newcastle United and Borussia Dortmund.

Both stalemates saw the Gunners fail to hold onto and build on one-goal advantages in the first half, before their foes came out all guns blazing after the restart and capitalised on Arsenal's alarming lack of a ruthless attacking touch.

Only four of Arsenal's 30 shots on goal in the Champions League were on target, as their 12-game winning run in home league phase/group stage fixtures came to an end, and their 17 Premier League goals scored so far ranks as the worst among all top-six teams.

However, the holders are five from five at the Emirates Stadium in the top flight - scoring 10 times and conceding just twice in the process - and they are yet to draw a blank at home in any tournament this term.

Interestingly, Arsenal's 10 home goals matches Man City's 10 away strikes in the 2026-27 Premier League season, while only Brighton & Hove Albion (26) can better the visitors' overall total of 22.

Such statistics will come as little consolation to travelling fans amid the Sky Blues' sorry slump, though, as Enzo Maresca's men have collected just one point from the last 12 on offer in the top flight after a perfect seven from seven to start the campaign.

The Citizens at least managed to snap their three-game losing sequence in last week's 1-1 draw at home to Fulham - not that such a feat was worth celebrating, though - before they also had to settle for a point in their midweek Champions League clash with Napoli.

Maresca and former Man City players have disagreed over whether the club's guilty verdict and appeal uncertainty over their 115 charges is impacting on-field performances, but the manager himself now finds himself under fire for questionable tactical calls and team selections over the autumnal period.

There is no suggestion that the former Chelsea boss is under any immediate sack pressure, though, despite presiding over a 122-year worst; City are just the second team in English Football League history to win their first seven matches of a season but fail to triumph in any of their next four, after the 1904-05 Sheffield Wednesday crop.

Furthermore, the Sky Blues were swatted aside in August's 3-0 Community Shield defeat to Arsenal, who have only lost two of their last nine head-to-heads against Man City and are unbeaten in their last three meetings on Emirates soil.

Fears of a serious shoulder injury to Arsenal number one David Raya have been allayed by Arteta, and at the time of writing, the Spain international has not been officially ruled out of the visit of Man City.

Arsenal will also welcome teenage wonderkid Max Dowman back from a three-game domestic suspension, but Martin Zubimendi (hamstring) and Bukayo Saka (quad) will not be back until just before Christmas at the earliest.

After Christos Tzolis's underwhelming midweek display, expect Eberechi Eze to return to the forward line, where Arteta has a critical choice to make between Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz after the former's thunderous finish in midweek.

Meanwhile, captain Martin Odegaard has another Premier League record in his sights; if he sets up two goals here, he will equal the record for the most assists by a Norwegian player in the competition - his 38 is marginally inferior to Morten Gamst Pedersen's 40.

Meanwhile, Man City are expected to head south with a fully-fit squad barring former Arsenal transfer target Antoine Semenyo, who is a few weeks away from returning from a knee injury.

Snubbed from the starting XI against Fulham before saving City's skin against Napoli, Rayan Cherki has surely done enough to hold his spot at the Emirates, while Jeremy Doku and Iliman Ndiaye also have cases to come back in after providing assists off the bench last time out.

Goalless in his last three Premier League matches, Erling Haaland could equal his own personal worst for an English top-flight goal drought, having never gone longer than four Premier League games without finding the back of the net.

Raya; Timber, Konsa, Gabriel, Calafiori; Guimaraes, Rice; Madueke, Odegaard, Eze; Havertz

Manchester City possible starting lineup:

Donnarumma; Nunes, Guehi, Dias, O'Reilly; Anderson, Fernandez; Ndiaye, Cherki, Doku; Haaland

The defensive numbers make for dreadful reading for Man City, who have let in seven goals across their last three away games and are without a clean sheet in 10 fixtures in total.

A profligate Arsenal side may not be the best-placed to capitalise, as only one of their last five wins has been by more than a one-goal margin, but the champions should still demonstrate why they are champions and deal another blow to Man City's already-fading title hopes.

Indeed, Tuttomercatoweb (via MilanNews) reports that they are also set to battle for Alejandro Balde. The Barcelona defender is likely to head away from Catalonia, and has been for some time, with Italy seeming like a possible destination.

It’s also worth noting that several Premier League clubs have taken an interest in the Spaniard, so the Italian route may not be the only one open to him.

#1661. Sampdoria swept aside by rampant Napoli – are the Partenopei on course for their first Scudetto in 26 years?

Home » Home 2 » Sampdoria swept aside by rampant Napoli – are the Partenopei on course for their first Scudetto in 26 years?

Dries Mertens celebrating with his team-mates on the touchline after his decisive goal in the 4-2 victory at Sampdoria is typical of the spirit and togetherness that has seen Napoli storm to the top of the Serie A title. It was in dedication to Chelsea loanee Nathaniel Chabolah who recently lost his mother a a nice touch to show that there is much more to life than football, even though they have put themselves in a wonderful position to end Juventusa dominance and end a 26-year wait for the Scudetto.

Five straight wins have put Maurizio Sarria s team two points clear at the top, with the former Empoli manager breathing a new lease of life throughout a team that have always looked capable of competing for the title, yet ultimately fallen short when the pressure to deliver grew. He has transformed the entire dynamics of how Napoli play, with clinical attacking movement combined with a rock-solid defence within a 4-3-3 system that is getting the very best from the players at his disposal. This seasona s statistics proved that point; Napoli are far and away the highest scorers in Serie A this season, while only Inter Milan and Juventus have a better defensive record. Just one defeat in the twenty league games since the opening day loss at Sassuolo is another illustration of just how good Napoli have been this season, with the crushing 4-0 win at AC Milan in early October a sign of what the Partenopei are truly capable of.

Juventus were always likely to be favourites for the Scudetto on Coral and any other football odds site as their dominance of Italian football threatens to extend into its fifth season, so it is perhaps refreshing from a purista s perspective that Napoli have emerged as real contenders to challenge the Bianconeri. Massimo Allegria s side have stormed up the table in ominous fashion following a surprisingly slow start to the season, with eleven straight victories serving a serious warning to Napoli that they will make them fight all the way for the 2015/2016 Serie A title. It remains to be seen how Sarri and his team handle the pressure of having Juventus breathing down their necks, but the fact they have scored twelve goals in their last three games would indicate that

Some may have been surprised by Gonzalo Higuaina s decision to swap Real Madrid for Naples in the summer of 2013, but the 28-year-old has become one of the most feared strikers in Italy. The Argentine international has formed a wonderful strikeforce at the front of a three-man attack, with Jose Callejon and Lorenzo Insigne adding searing pace and skill on either side of a frontman who has made a career from being a true predator inside the box.

Twenty-one games in as many Serie A games this season puts him amongst the most in-form strikers in world football, with his clinical finish which opened the scoring against Sampdoria proving just how good he has been in front of goal. It is the sort of purple patch that any striker worth their salt would dream to be in; Coral have unsurprisingly backed Higuain as favourite to score in their next game against Sarria s former employers Empoli who have kept just one clean sheet from their last five league fixtures. Napoli will need Higuain to carry his rich vein of form throughout the rest of the season if they are to have any chance of maintaining their wonderful pace and sprint clear of the chasing pack.

Napoli have won many admirers across Europe for the quality of football they have played this season, but it remains to be seen if they have the mentality to pass the acid test and keep the momentum going between now and the end of the season. Recent history would suggest that their chances are not great; the Partenopei, then managed by Walter Mazzarri, put themselves in a wonderful position in 2012/2013, only to finish runners-up behind Juventus as the odd slip at the wrong times proved costly in their pursuit of Juventus. A number of third-placed finishes would also suggest that Napoli have lacked the mentality and guile to end their long wait for a Scudetto, but there is real excitement in Naples that the current crop of players have what it takes to stop the Old Lady from making it five titles in a row.

#1660. EPL Prepares for Most Exciting Title Race in Years

Home » Home 2 » EPL Prepares for Most Exciting Title Race in Years

Now that all of the top four English Premier League teams have had a chance to play each other, we find ourselves looking at one of the most wide open title races in recent memory. As of this writing, the league leaders are only separated by a mere six points. With the exception of Manchester City, we could very well see a new face hoisting the Premier League trophy at the end of the season.

For much of the year, it looked like Arsenal would be in the running for its first league title in more than a decade. With the Gunners’ recent victory against Leicester City, they are very much back in the conversation. Danny Welbeck returned to the pitch for the first time this season and made an immediate impact for Arsene Wenger’s squad, scoring the last-minute, game-winning goal to propel the team to within two points of the top spot. Given that even more key players are set to return to action for Arsenal in the coming months, this is easily the best shot they have had of winning a championship since their undefeated 2003-04 season.

Another surprise team that certainly deserves its own mention is Tottenham Hotspur. Following the club’s controversial defeat of Manchester City, the Spurs sit in second place, a mere two points behind Leicester City and ahead of Arsenal on goal differential. Tottenham have yet to win a title in the Premier League era and they have not won an English championship since 1961. The team has done a superb job of backing up star striker Harry Kane with a glut of promising young players, and their goal tally only helps to reinforce the wisdom behind the strategy of manager Mauricio Pochettino.

Meanwhile, Manchester City is still hoping to snag its third title as something of a swan song for exiting manager Manuel Pellegrini. It was recently announced that the club had hired Pep Guardiola . from Bayern Munich to take charge of the team beginning with next season. Thus, Pellegrini has been forced to endure the rest of the campaign as a dead man walking. Despite the impending exit of Pellegrini, City are still in the race for the Premier League title in addition to both the F.A. Cup and Champions League. Theoretically, the club could pull off a treble, if it can manage a solid string of performances during the final half of the season.

At the beginning of the season, it was expected that the usual suspects would once again dominate the league. Many predicted the reigning champs at Chelsea to repeat their success. However, a shocking season has seen the team part ways with controversial manager Jose Mourinho and struggle to remain in the top half of the tables with hopes of a Champions League spot dashed long ago.

For the first time in years, there’s a chance to see a completely new team win the league. No matter which club you support, there’s no denying that this has made for one of the most thrilling contests in recent memory. In a league where money talks, small fish like Leicester City are surprising everyone, and we can only hope that this means a new era of parity for the Premier League.

#1659. Dortmund a tricky test + Guimaraes on getting to grips with Arteta’s midfield

Arsenal are in Champions League action this evening, taking on Borussia Dortmund at home. It’s a game that Kepa Arrizabalaga will start in the absence of David Raya, but the news around the Arsenal number 1 was a little more positive than expected. In his press conference yesterday, Mikel Arteta said:

He’s not fit for tomorrow, unfortunately, but it doesn’t look too serious. We need some more tests tomorrow, but it’s quite encouraging. With the pain that he was showing immediately after the action, we were all quite worried, but he seems to be better than what we expected.

We expected something much worse because he could almost not handle the amount of pain that he had at that moment, and the first test that we’ve done showed something that is much more encouraging. There’s no need for surgery, which was the main fear especially because that would rule him out for months, so let’s see.

So, it seems like he’s going to miss a few games, but not anything prolonged, which is obviously good news. Elsewhere, there’s room for rotation, and I think this might be a good chance to give minutes to William Saliba who hasn’t played competitively since the World Cup.  He’s had a couple of behind closed doors appearances, which will be useful in terms of fitness, but nothing compares with actually playing at this level.

I wonder too if players like Ben White, Cristhian Mosquera and Piero Hincapie will fancy their chances, but that seems like a lot of change in the back four – and the goalkeeper – so we’ll have to wait and see there. In midfield, we can bring Myles Lewis-Skelly in for a start, but obviously the manager has plenty to choose from in there, and up front I imagine it will be a chance for Viktor Gyokeres whose minutes have been scant so far this season. Asked if the striker had been knocking on his door about that, Arteta said:

No, we have conversations with every player to make sure that they understand what we are doing, to gather information about the way they are feeling, and so far, it’s been very positive with Viktor and with the rest of the team.

He could really use a goal tonight if he does start, as does Christos Tzolis whose numbers so far this season aren’t where you’d like them to be. Obviously there’s more to assessing a player than simply goals and assists, but for a left winger brought into replace two players who contributed a lot to the team over the last few seasons, just two assists from 11 appearances (Community Shield excluded) is a little below what you’d hope. He has had an injury, of course, but if his season needs a kick-start, tonight would be very timely.

Dortmund sit top of the Bundesliga right now, unbeaten in the league thus far, and with just one defeat all season in all competitions. That did come in the Champions League, away to Bodo Glimt, but this will be a tricky test tonight for Arsenal. Arteta says:

I’m very impressed with them, you see the results so far, where they are in the Bundesliga at the top and where they are in the Champions League and especially the way they are playing, the way they are dominating games, the amount of threat they are able to create. We had them here in pre-season, and they showed the quality and what they are capable of, so we are very much aware of that. But we play at home in front of our crowd, and now we’re going to go and attack the game, that’s for sure.

After a disappointing second half against Newcastle on Saturday, I’m sure the manager will be looking for a response from his side. It’s nice to be at home again, and a long spell of games in London will hopefully less taxing physically without all the travel, so it’d be good to get that off to a winning start tonight.

Elsewhere, Bruno Guimaraes spoke about his first few months at the club, and how he now feels like he’s getting to grips with what Mikel Arteta wants from him, saying:

I’m here, I don’t know, three, four months? It’s still a lot to go, but I now definitely understand my role in the team, the way that Mikel wants me to play in the team. So, yeah, I think I still can play much, much better.

And it’s quite interesting to hear him talk about how at Arsenal he is more ‘free’ than he was under Eddie Howe at Newcastle. Most would feel it was the other way around, but he explained:

It’s very different. When I was at Newcastle, you play more positional, keep more your position. Here it’s a little bit more free.

If you see the game against Newcastle, they were marking us man to man. You see JT [Jurrien Timber] plays a six, an eight and a number nine sometimes, so you have to move a lot. Of course, I was not used to it. So now I understand a little bit more what he wants for the midfield.

I think there’s more to come from him, he’s looked good at times, a little off the pace at others, and I think my main worry is about the physical side of his game. Does he have the running power and athleticism that enables players like Declan Rice and Martin Odegaard to thrive under this manager? At 29, he’s no spring chicken, but I guess there’s always room for improvement. Anyway, his press conference stuff from yesterday is worth reading, and there’s some good chat about him on the Arsecast Extra which you’ll find below.

Right, I’ll leave it there for this morning. As ever, we’ll bring you live blog coverage of the game later, as well all the post-game stuff on Arseblog News like the match report, player ratings, manager reaction, quotes round-up and more. Don’t forget the updated Arseblog apps also have a cool new matchday centre, full of stats, alerts, and much more.

#1658. Kevin De Bruyne insists potential punishment over Man City's guilty verdict will not tarnish his old club's achievements under Pep Guardiola - or diminish his 'love' for the owners

Published: 16:01 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 16:04 EST, 23 November 2026

Manchester City legend Kevin De Bruyne insisted that any potential punishment for breaching financial rules will not change what Pep Guardiola’s team achieved and their memories of success.

The Belgian was a key pillar during the spell of unprecedented domestic dominance and has a statue commissioned outside the Etihad Stadium.

De Bruyne is back in town with Napoli for Tuesday’s Champions League tie, reiterating his ‘love’ for City and its owners, while revealing recent talks with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak.

The 35-year-old brushed off suggestions that silverware collected during his decade at City would be tarnished if the club lost their appeal and were sanctioned after being found guilty of the vast majority of charges levelled at them.

De Bruyne’s trophy haul – six Premier League titles, one Champions League, two FA Cups and five Carabao Cups – were largely secured outside of the nine-year period in which City were scrutinised, up to 2018.

‘I’m proud of what I've done as a football player,’ De Bruyne said. ‘Honestly, this is my club, I love the owners. I've talked about a lot of stuff outside football (with them), I've even spoken to Khaldoon about how to buy a club and everything.

The 36-year-old brushed off suggestions that silverware collected during his decade at City would be tarnished if the club lost their appeal

‘It (stripping of titles) still doesn't change (anything), my football has not changed. I don't think a lot of people will change in their mind how they view me as a player, or how we played.

‘But everybody has his own opinion and other people may be disgraced a bit. I can't change anything about that.’

De Bruyne’s final two seasons at City were plagued by injury before he joined Napoli on a free transfer in 2025 and his first return in last year’s Champions League lasted just 26 minutes as he hobbled off.

Classed as the greatest player in the club’s modern history, De Bruyne was typically forthright on the uncertainty surrounding his former employers after the guilty verdicts read by a three-person independent commission.

‘My feelings have never been different,’ he added. ‘Honestly, the way that I feel is just the way that I've been treated by this club, what I've done with this club for me personally, and how we've worked together as a group.

‘Of course, it's a lot of things that have been going on. I have nothing but affection for this club, and that will never change. Even now, the people who treated me and my family for 10 years is the most important thing.’

De Bruyne left City under duress, vehemently disagreeing with the club’s decision not to offer him a new contract following a spate of injuries before choosing Napoli – and his long-term future in Serie A is now appearing in doubt.

All eyes in Italy were on the midfielder’s public response to an interview published with his wife, Michele, in which she was reported to have criticised life in Naples and yearned for a move away. Those comments were taken out of context, according to a visibly frustrated De Bruyne, with PSV Eindhoven looking at securing a transfer in January.

De Bruyne left City under duress but revealed recent talks with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak

But City supporters will have been more interested in how far De Bruyne went in backing their club ahead of next month’s appeal hearing.

‘In life there are rules, but everybody plays to the limit, I would say,’ he claimed, seemingly referring to how financial rules are interpreted by the Premier League’s elite clubs.

‘I played in between the white lines, and I competed with other players, and I had many experiences with my teams.

‘So for me that's the thing that I value most. The most important thing is the relationships between everybody that I had and how you manage these things, and I've given my all.’

De Bruyne smirked as he discussed how he knew exactly how City would attack Napoli given his knowledge of the club and manager Enzo Maresca, who was Guardiola’s assistant during the 2023 Treble campaign.

Maresca is facing criticism after three defeats and a draw in their last four league games. The Italian called for calm over recent performances and believes that the transition from Guardiola was always going to represent a bumpy road.

‘It's like a reset, a restart, after 10 years with the same manager, same face, same words, same method,’ Maresca said.

‘It's not easy to all of a sudden change. For me personally, it's all normal, and hopefully as soon as possible we can find the right balance in all the lines - defensive, midfield - and we can be consistent, which for me is the difference between us and other clubs.’

#1656. Arsenal predicted lineup vs. Man City: David Raya decision made as Viktor Gyokeres dropped

By Ben Knapton | 27 Nov 2026 11:33, Last updated: 27 Nov 2026 11:43

Arsenal goalkeeper David Raya is believed to be in with a chance of facing Manchester City in Sunday's Premier League blockbuster at the Emirates Stadium.

The Spain international sustained a serious-looking shoulder injury in last weekend's 2-2 draw with Newcastle United, but his issue is nowhere near as severe as first believed.

Mikel Arteta is yet to rule Raya out of the visit of Man City, and if the Gunners' number one is declared fit enough to participate, he will undoubtedly steal the gloves off of Kepa Arrizabalaga.

Whoever starts in goal for Arsenal should be shielded by the central pairing of Ezri Konsa and Gabriel Magalhaes, as William Saliba is slowly re-integrated, and the full-back duo of Jurrien Timber and Riccardo Calafiori, displacing Ben White and Piero Hincapie after the 1-1 draw with Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League in midweek.

Myles Lewis-Skelly should also make way for Bruno Guimaraes in the double pivot, while the underwhelming Christos Tzolis can expect to lose out to Eberechi Eze on the left flank.

Noni Madueke and Martin Odegaard are safe, though, as the latter chases Morten Gamst Pedersen's record of 40 Premier League assists from a Norwegian player; the Arsenal skipper sits on 38.

Viktor Gyokeres's thunderbolt in midweek has given Arteta a major decision to make up top, but Premier League regular Kai Havertz - who has scored three goals and set up another in his last four matches against Man City - should come back in.

#1653. The Rock of London: Looking back at John Terry’s Chelsea FC career

Home » Home 2 » The Rock of London: Looking back at John Terry’s Chelsea FC career

At the start of this season, John Terry leaving Chelsea was the last thing on anyone’s mind. All was rosy at Stamford Bridge, the home of the newly crowed English champions. In over 21 years at the club, there was no indication that Terry would not retire a Chelsea man.

The Blues’ skipper’s announcement in January 2016, then, came as a shock to the Chelsea faithful, bringing notice to the seemingly premature — even if inevitable — fall of the curtain on a legendary career.

After making his debut in the League Cup against Aston Villa late in 1998, John Terry made sporadic appearances under Gianluca Vialli, before joining Nottingham Forest on a short loan spell. He broke into the first team in 2000-01, when manager Claudio Ranieri handed him 22 Premier League appearances during a season that the 20-year-old would finish as the club’s Player of the Year.

It would be the first of several achievements to come.

Terry’s importance to the team grew as Ranieri relied on his partnership with then-captain Marcel Desailly to mastermind Chelsea’s progression from a fashionable mid-table club to a Champions League team that meant business. They received a major shot in the arm when Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich bought the club in 2003. It was also a significant year in Terry’s international career as he made his England debut against Serbia and Montenegro in June.

The season that followed saw Chelsea finish above perennial winners Manchester United for the first time in Premier League history, and defeat Premiership invincibles Arsenal en route to the club’s first Champions League semifinal. Terry ended the season making a first of four appearances in the PFA Team of the Year, and went to Portugal for the European Championships having displaced Sol Campbell as England’s first choice centre-back.

In the summer of 2004, Chelsea brought in Jose Mourinho, who was fresh from winning a treble with the unfancied FC Porto and raring to take on bigger challenges. The 23-year-old Terry was named captain as Chelsea embarked on the most successful period in the club’s history. In the three seasons that followed, Chelsea won 2 league cups, 2 Premier League titles and the FA Cup — success built on a core of John Terry, Frank Lampard, Petr Cech and Didier Drogba, Chelsea’s ‘old guard’.

This was also a period when Terry picked up several individual accolades. He was named PFA Player of the Year in 2005, the first defender to win the award since Paul McGrath in 1993. He would make a first of five consecutive appearances in the FIFPro World XI in 2005, as well as a first of four appearances in the UEFA Team of the Year.

He was also voted Chelsea’s Player of the Year for the second time in his career in 2006. Steve McClaren, hired as England manager after an underwhelming 2006 World Cup, named the Chelsea skipper as England captain.

Terry was now, beyond argument, one of football’s best.

However, more testing times were to come.

September 2007 saw the departure of Mourinho after a falling out with the club board. The season itself promised much but left a Chelsea squad dejected on three occasions as they saw the League Cup, the Premier League and the Champions League trophies go elsewhere.

For the European Cup in particular, Terry was left with no one but himself to blame as he slipped for the crucial penalty, a moment he has said will haunt him forever. Chelsea and Terry experienced further European heartbreak the following season as Tom Henning Ovrebo had a refereeing performance to forget at Stamford Bridge, handing Barcelona a berth in the final and eventually the trophy.

In early 2010, when he was revealed as the English footballer who had an affair with Vanessa Perroncel, Wayne Bridge’s ex-girlfriend — a horrendous personal error that cost him his status as England captain — it made him the perennial recipient of passionate booing across English grounds. After the revelation, Chelsea travelled to Burnley. Amidst a frosty reception, he scored a late winner to put Carlo Ancelotti’s side back on track in the title race, one they would go on to win in some style. All of this typified John Terry — imperfect, but unshakeable.

Terry had built an unflappable reputation as a top class defender, leader and hard man. He said about himself, “I still say if the ball is there to be won I will go for it, whether with my head or whatever, and if it means us scoring or stopping a goal, I won’t think twice.”

The period that followed, however, was not good for Chelsea or their captain. The team finished the 2010-11 season trophyless, and Carlo Ancelotti paid for it with his job. This was the first of two times in Terry’s career where he and his club would have an extremely underwhelming season following a dominant one, and it also marked the first attempt to phase him out of the first team.

New manager Andre Villas-Boas attempted to introduce a high defensive line that left Terry exposed on a number of occasions, and saw the young Portuguese manager fall back on quicker defenders to implement his system. He was also determined to make lesser use of Frank Lampard and displace Didier Drogba with Fernando Torres. These were unpopular moves that led to poor results and eventually his sacking. Terry was not helped by another personal abberation, mouthing racial profanity at Anton Ferdinand of QPR, an act that saw him land a lengthy ban and damage his position in the England squad almost beyond repair.

Interim manager Roberto Di Matteo reinstated the old guard, and was rewarded with the ultimate prize — the first Champions League in Chelsea’s history.

Terry retired from international football following EURO 2012, leaving him to focus on his club career. However, further rotation was to follow during the reign of Rafael Benitez, who played Terry only in games of lesser importance. This was something he could do with relative impunity owing to the fact that his stock could not have fallen any further among Chelsea fans.

The writing was seemingly on the wall, however. Unsavoury incidents were fresher in the memory than individual accolades, the skipper was out of favour for two seasons running, and was well over 30 years of age. Was John Terry done?

Mourinho did not share the views of Benitez and Villas-Boas. Where they saw a slowing, easily-exposed has-been, he saw an experienced warrior with an excellent reading of the game who could form a title-winning partnership with the quicker Gary Cahill.

Terry grabbed the opportunity he was handed with gusto, performing with excellence in Mourinho’s lower defensive block. The English pair formed the core of a defence that would go on to win the club’s fourth Premier League title in 2015, leading the table from the opening day to the end. It was a landmark achievement for Terry in particular as he played every minute of a league campaign for the first time in his career, aged 34.

Once again they tried to put him down. Once again he fed off it and rose tall.

Chelsea did not start the defence of their title well at all, gathering just 4 points from the first 4 matches. Mourinho, who asked Terry to take the club on his shoulders in 2004 and stood by him for two seasons in his second stint, hauled off his skipper at half-time at the Etihad in the second game of the season, and began to rotate him out of the team, giving an increasing number of starts to the young Kurt Zouma.

The season did not take much of a turn for the better even under interim manager Guus Hiddink, particularly in a defensive sense as the Blues continued to let in goals during a meek climb to the top half of the table, with or without Terry in the side.

A sending off at the Stadium of Light following an injury layoff is not the kind of ending that the fans desired for their beloved captain, who has emerged from the dugout 703 times in Chelsea colours and has been the face of the club through the most successful period in their history.

Offered a new deal by the club last week, the skipper responded, “The contract extension the club has offered me is a different role and I hope everyone will understand I want to take the time to consider it carefully before making a decision.” While fans will hope — for reasons emotional as well as those to do with football — that Terry stays on, the chances look slim.

Should the captain leave the ship, the Blues supporters’ emotions are best summed up by a certain banner that embellishes the Shed End: Captain, Leader, Legend.

#1652. Arsenal 1-1 Dortmund: Familiar flaws hold Arsenal back

A 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League on Tuesday raised some very familiar concerns and, if we’re being honest, revealed nothing we didn’t already know.

Arsenal can play world-class football and completely dominate teams for long spells, but lack the world-class attack to make the most of that domination, the sort of players you just know will create and convert big chances when the time comes. And the way the team is starting games after the break is worrying, with teams who are battered to within an inch of their lives early on suddenly able to compete.

I really feel like I could write two versions of today’s blog. One where I’m miserable, of course: the players can’t shoot, they make all the wrong choices in the decisive moment, we can’t keep wasting chances and dropping off after the break, if Andrea Berta doesn’t deliver the true heirs to Thierry Henry and Robert Pires in January, then he should be stuffed into one of the cannons outside the Armoury and fired into the cold night air.

The other version is much more glass half full: Arteta is coaching masterclasses every week, this level of dominance in games is something I could only dream of a few years ago, that’s the most shots we’ve had in a game all season, we’re top of the league, we’re creating loads without any set-piece reliance and without Bukayo Saka – the goals will come.

Some people reading this would prefer (and relate better to) one version, and others the other version, I’m sure. Let’s see where we end up!

There were, as there tends to be in these Champions League games, a fair few changes from the weekend. Kepa, Piero Hincapie, Ben White, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Christos Tzolis, and Viktor Gyokeres all came into the team.

Despite featuring half a different side, there were plenty of parallels with the Newcastle match. Arsenal were dominant from the off, with Hincapie and White taking turns to play off of Gyokeres. Dortmund had no idea how to cover them and both fullbacks were the targets of early crosses into the box.

After a couple of long-range efforts, Arsenal got their goal they deserved, with Gyokeres launching a ferocious, dipping effort beyond Gregor Kobel. The Swede can put his foot through the ball, that’s for sure, and the Dortmund backline gave him the sort of time and space to set himself that he doesn’t often get.

The pressure continued after the opener for a while, with Tzolis forcing a good save and Madueke just unable to sort his feet to tap in the rebound.

It’s fair to say the game settled down after 15/20 minutes, with Dortmund growing into it a little, but it was still Arsenal who looked like scoring the next goal. Rice shot over from almost the same patch of grass Gyokeres had scored from, and the midfielder had another chance when a beautiful one-touch move ended with him bursting through, hurtling towards the Dortmund box. Maybe he could’ve picked out Madueke in support, but he went alone and Nico Schlotterbeck just got across to block the shot.

Another huge chance was denied by the offside flag as much as the finishing – Madueke won the ball high, Odegaard squared it to Gyokeres, and the Swede fired over from near the penalty spot. Odegaard was ruled offside but I’m not convinced: had the ball hit the net, I think we’d have seen a very tight VAR check.

There was one thought on everyone’s minds at half-time: don’t do the same thing again. After Slavia Prague and Newcastle, do not do the same thing again.

There was an early warning sign with Dortmund sliding the ball across the box and Maximilian Beier kicking the air. He didn’t make the same mistake with his next opportunity. Centre-back Joane Gadou (who was very impressive all evening) charged through the heart of the pitch before playing the ball to Beier, who jinked to unbalance Gabriel and slotted home.

Sometimes a goal is just a good goal, and I don’t think anyone was really at fault here. It’s a great run from Gadou, Beier tricks Gabriel to take the ball onto his weaker left side – it’s fair if Gabriel is expecting (and blocking the angle) on the attacker’s favoured foot, I know how that can happen. I think if we score that goal we’re talking about two brilliant individuals, rather than defensive errors.

My first thought? Not again. My second? OK, how do we respond? Because on Saturday, the response was poor.

This time it was a lot better. Jobe Bellingham had a rebound disallowed for offside, a moment that really brought the crowd back into the game, but in truth, that was Dortmund’s only real moment of threat. From the goal on 55 minutes to full-time, Arsenal had 15 shots to Dortmund’s two.

And that doesn’t include Serhou Guirassy playing one-twos with the post after a clever, low free-kick from Martin Odegaard late on.

Madueke had an effort blocked. Gyokeres flicked a header wide. Madueke shot wide beyond the far post after a good run. Gyokeres missed a big chance with his head from six yards out. Rice hit the near post from a tight angle after a brilliant pass from Eberechi Eze.

A couple of late corners came to nothing, and that was it.

Mikel Arteta was clearly pleased with the performance on the whole:

Well, I think I love the way the team played. There’s no question how superior, how dominant, how much of a threat we were, how connected everybody was to the game … It was great to watch. It was unbelievable that sometimes the ball hasn’t ended up in the back of the net. That’s my feeling.

to do what we’ve done out there is just something to be very, very pleased about, because there is very little more that we can demand from the team.

But we all know what that little more is:

obviously the feeling is that we should reward ourselves much more when you put that kind of performance, the amount of chances, the situation, and even shots that are not there. We are three against two, two against one, and the ball doesn’t land with the right person. There is an element of luck, there is an element of us finishing the actions better. We need to insist, because I think what the team has done and shown today is the right direction.

Often when Arsenal don’t win games, it feels like it’s because the team haven’t created enough chances. We end up focusing on that one moment, where that one player didn’t execute the way you wanted. But last night wasn’t one of those: Arsenal didn’t struggle to turn dominance into good, slick football, and that football into a healthy number of decent opportunities.

That’s incredibly frustrating, but I do think you win a lot more often than not when you do that. Maybe that’s a hard sell for some this morning, but it’s how I feel about it when we play well, especially when we’ve been winning games anyway. That’s the first time this season we’ve gone two without a win across all competitions, and we’ve won 14 of 19 games so far. Sometimes things don’t fall for you, and this one felt a lot like ‘one of those’, certainly more than Newcastle did.

A word for a couple of promising performances too, with the boss asked about Gyokeres in his post-match press conference:

What I love the most is how connected he was to the team. We used him many times in different ways. His link-up play, the way he held the ball, the way he threw it in behind and stretched the pitch. There was a lot to like in that performance and that’s the victory that we need.

His finishing was off after the brilliant opener, but at least he was in the positions: too often this season and last, Gyokeres has gone through a game barely registering a shot. He had seven last night, and if he can do that more often he’ll score a lot more. His general play was improved too, both holding the ball up and competing in behind.

And I thought Martin Odegaard was excellent too. His eight chances created from open play was the most of any player in any Champions League match so far this season.

Since we returned to the competition in 2023, we’ve had a player create more than five chances in a match just twice: Odegaard at Napoli in September (6) and Odegaard last night (9). He’s incredibly unlucky not to be leaving the game with a couple of assists.

The draw leaves us in a decent position to finish in the all-important top eight in the league phase still, although you have to squint a bit to see us landing in the also-important top two. Real Madrid are up next and that’s a reminder of the sort of teams we’re up against: finishing in the top two is a tall order at the best of times.

With each passing game, it is impossible not to wonder what could be done in January to add to the team. Unless there’s a sudden uptick out of nowhere, those thoughts aren’t disappearing. And even if there is a massive uptick, those thoughts will still be around. But 30 shots is the most we’ve had in a game all season, and the same group of players have scored more goals with fewer shots (/chances) plenty of times. Let’s hope we see some more clinical finishing on Sunday.

Guess I landed on the glass half full version.

There should be an Arsecast once Blogs has caught up with the game, so stay tuned for that. Enjoy your Wednesdays!

#1650. Fat margins

Thanks to Lewis for taking care of the blog yesterday as I was unable to watch the Borussia Dortmund match live. I saw that we’d scored early but only saw the final score well after the full-time whistle, so I guess it was a little disappointing not to have built on that fantastic hit from Viktor Gyokeres.

I think while I have some frustrations overall with our inability to turn dominance into goals, I’m more comfortable with it when we’re actually making chances. I think the manager would have a far bigger issue on his hands if we weren’t, and on Tuesday night the fact we had 30 attempts on goal tells you the problem isn’t chance creation, it’s about being clinical.

It wasn’t that long ago that it was the other way around. We found it hard to make goalscoring opportunities and for me that’s much more of a worry. It doesn’t mean we can’t improve, it doesn’t mean January becomes any less important the closer it gets, it’s just that the solution lies with the players we have who should be capable of better. There were a couple of other opportunities for Gyokeres that could easily have made this a better night for him and for Arsenal, Declan Rice hit the post, fine margins that shouldn’t be impossible to squeeze in our favour. Make ’em wider, thicker.

In the end though, I think the bottom line is quality of personnel. Over the last few seasons the only front three player we’ve had who looked like he could become top, top quality was Bukayo Saka. He was certainly on that trajectory until injuries became a real hindrance, and we saw that this season there were modifications made to his game to make him more effective. I know the discourse around him was a little polarised, but I saw a player more involved, who looked sharper and capable of producing the kind of volume that made him so impactful.

Saka isn’t one of those who finishes every chance he gets, he’s a guy who just keeps going until he makes something happen. The hamstring injury, and then the ongoing Achilles issue made it harder for him to contribute, but I really was encouraged by his season until the injury he sustained against Bayern. And it’s interesting to me that while it might be the kind of player he is anyway, we’ve basically asked Noni Madueke to replicate ‘Old Saka’ in terms of that kind of volume of shots and crosses. He’s had 11 shots across the last two games, and perhaps a single goal from those appear to be a scant return, I think it’s how we need him to play and how Arsenal can maximise what we’ve got up front.

There was an interesting comment on the Arses yesterday wondering how it is that Mikel Arteta can coach and improve defenders and midfielders so well, but not do the same with his attacking players. Some will say it’s because he’s a coach who is defensively minded and this is his wheelhouse. This is what he’s good at. Make a great defence, build a solid midfield in front of them. Perhaps there’s an element of truth in that, but for me it’s down to the players he has to work with.

If the raw ingredients are good, the recipe has a much better chance of being good, regardless of the talent of the chef. If you get to work with players like Ben White, William Saliba, Gabriel, Riccardo Calafiori, Declan Rice, Martin Odegaard etc, all of whom arrived in at a relatively young age (Rice perhaps the exception because he had a lot of experience, but Arteta has still made him better), you can develop that potential, build relationships, and see that come to fruition on the pitch.

Up front though, I don’t think we’ve had that level of talent. What can you do with a Willian or a Marquinhos? What can you do with a Gabriel Jesus whose knee explodes (perhaps as we saw in those opening few months before injury hit, you could have done a lot more)? Was Gabriel Martinelli’s plateau down to Arteta’s coaching or the player’s ceiling? I think the fact he’s playing now in Saudi Arabia says a bit about that. I think Arteta squeezed a lot out of someone like Leandro Trossard, who arrived at 28 and became a better player than he was at Brighton, but ultimately there are limits. The same goes for our two strikers, Gyokeres and Kai Havertz. On their days, they can get you goals, but there are too many days when they won’t, and I don’t really think it’s a coaching issue.

We also need to remember that there was a season when Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal scored more goals than the Invincibles did when they won the league in 2004. It’s not as if his coaching, per se, is an impediment to scoring goals – but like anything it’s layered and multi-factored. We had to become more defensive when all of our attackers were basically banjaxed, we still managed to finish second that season when all we had on the bench was a end-stage Raheem Sterling. If that has tipped the balance a little too far the other way, then you can understand it, and Arsenal are the masters of the single-goal margin victory these days.

I think we can do more to score more, I think some of the players we have are capable of delivering more goals and assists, and over the next few months – being realistic about what we might do in January – that’s what we need to lean into. But my gut feeling is that until such time as we have better attackers to work with, this will remain an issue – and it’s worth saying that said issue is one we still find a way to achieve success with more often than that.

I’d just like some fat margins once in a while.

Having arrived at the Hungarian club in January 2025, initially on loan before signing permanently, the Guinean has failed to regain a regular place in the team. His last start was on 20 September. Since then, he has been a substitute on two occasions, but has mainly been absent from the squad.

Keita's absence comes as Ferencvaros make an excellent start to their Europa League campaign, with four wins in as many matches, including a convincing 2-0 victory over AC Milan.

Above all, Keita's current difficulties are nothing new.

Recurring injuries had already disrupted his time at Liverpool (2018-2023), where he never managed to establish himself as an undisputed starter despite the expectations placed on him after his successful spell at RB Leipzig.

His stay at Werder Bremen then failed to relaunch his career. Physical problems continued to disrupt his consistency, before his relationship with the German club deteriorated. Having arrived at Ferencvaros in January 2025 on loan, then signing permanently a few months later, the Guinean hoped to rediscover continuity in Hungary. But once again, he has not been able to play more than 10 league matches per season so far.

It is to be hoped that this break will allow one of Guinea's greatest talents of the past decade to recharge, professionally and above all personally.

#1646. Paul Scholes says 'rabbit in headlights' Leny Yoro is not 'Premier League level' - as Nicky Butt claims this Man United side are the 'most unathletic team' in their history with only THREE players able to run at Anfield

Published: 16:03 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 16:05 EST, 23 November 2026

Former Manchester United midfielder Paul Scholes has become the latest ex-Red Devil to tear into the club's defence, criticising Leny Yoro following his red card in his side's 4-0 defeat by Liverpool.

Yoro was sent off less than eight minutes into United's clash with their rivals at Anfield on Sunday, tripping Alexander Isak as he ran in on goal after an error from Matthijs de Ligt.

He has had a mixed time of things since his £52million move to Old Trafford in 2024, though has been playing in a leaky United defence that has conceded 23 goals in 11 Premier League matches this season – with only Crystal Palace conceding more.

Several different members of United's defence have come under fire this season, and, on Monday, it was the turn of Yoro.

'The Premier League at this minute just looks a little bit too much for him,' Scholes said on The Good, The Bad and The Football, sponsored by Midnite.

He added: 'You know what, he’s come in to a really bad setup defensively now. I think they also made the point yesterday if he went in next to (Virgil) Van Dijk he might look a little bit better but he doesn’t look Premier League level. He looks like a rabbit in the headlights.'

Paul Scholes (pictured) has suggested Leny Yoro is not yet ready for the Premier League

Yoro was sent off in the opening minutes of Manchester United's 4-0 defeat by Liverpool

Fellow former United midfielder Nicky Butt, who played alongside Scholes for United between 1994 and 2004, added: 'If that’s Man United in our day, he’s on loan like a Jonny Evans or a John O’Shea. He’s a great talent that will come good.'

Scholes, though, wasn't having any of it.

He replied: 'I’m not sure how much of a great talent he is. I think he has shown a little bit of a sign in the France squad but every time I’ve seen him he doesn’t look at the races. Everything’s happening around him and he’s just a bit, oh, what do I do?'

United have also faced criticism for their apparent lack of running this season, with eyebrows raised when Youri Tielemans said in the summer that they didn't do much prior to the campaign getting under way.

The club rank 17th for distance covered in the top flight this season, with Liverpool, Brentford and Everton below them. The latter two will almost certainly pass them though after their game on Monday.

That, according to Butt, is down to the players.

'We’ve had our say about the players and they’re just not good enough,' he said. 'It is the most unathletic team I’ve ever seen in Man United.

'I’m going to go through a team and I’m trying to be as honest as I can. Forget the quality for right now. For me, physicality-wise, if you go through a team, the right back, he’s physically OK, but he’s not amazing. De Ligt or Harry, whoever he’s going to play in there, physically not great. Martinez for me is physically not great. You got Yoro who will physically come good.

Nicky Butt (pictured), meanwhile, has criticised the physical ability of many of United's players

'Then I go on to the midfield, none of them are physically good enough. Kobbie can get about the pitch 15-20 yards, but he’s not box to box. Said that numerous times. He’s got a lot of talent. He’s got a lot of things going for him. I think he’s a top player. He ain’t got the legs. He needs to have legs around him but his legs around him at the minute are Bruno and Tielemans - and they can’t run around.

'Look at Mbeumo, I think he’s OK but he’s not going to blow anybody away. I think Cunha can run. So then you look at the whole squad and you’re saying three players can run.

'What I’m getting at there, and it sounds like I’m being a draconian but what you have to do first and foremost when you go to Anfield is to be able to compete physically and they can’t so they have no chance.'
